title: Nonstabilizerness of quantum tensor network states is intractable in two dimensions
abstract: Nonstabilizerness is a necessary resource for quantum systems to lie beyond the classically simulable regime. With the advent of stabilizer $α$-Rényi entropies, nonstabilizerness has also become a many-body diagnostic, complementary to entanglement. While deciding whether an arbitrary quantum state has nonstabilizerness is provably hard, such states already require a description exponentially large in the number of qubits and are thus out of reach for many-body physics. Here we instead consider 2D tensor network (TN) states, which compactly capture states obeying an entanglement area law, and ask whether they admit a simpler algorithm for the same task. In contrast to the 1D case, we prove that, even at small, constant bond dimension, computing the stabilizer entropy of 2D TN states is $\# P$ hard for any integer $α\ge 2$, and deciding stabilizer membership is $\rm C_{=} P $ complete. Hence, under standard complexity assumptions, no classical or quantum algorithm with polynomial resources can solve either problem in the worst case. Both hardness results persist even when the problems are formulated up to constant additive accuracy.
summary: This paper proves that determining if a quantum state described by a 2D Tensor Network (PEPS) is nonstabilizable, or even just checking if it is a stabilizer state, is computationally extremely hard. The hardness results show that these problems are at least as hard as counting problems ($\#	ext{P}$) or solving $	ext{C}=	ext{P}$ problems. This implies that no efficient classical or quantum algorithm can solve these diagnostics for general 2D quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper determines the computational complexity of quantifying nonstabilizerness for quantum states represented by 2D Tensor Networks (PEPS).
main_result: Both computing the Stabilizer Entropy (SE) and deciding stabilizer membership for 2D PEPS are proven to be computationally hard, specifically $\#	ext{P}$-hard and $	ext{C}=	ext{P}$-complete, respectively.
method: The hardness results are established via reductions from known hard computational problems, such as $	ext{C}=	ext{P}$ languages, to the evaluation of SE or the stabilizer membership test on PEPS.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum many-body states described by Projected Entangled Pair States (PEPS) on a 2D lattice, which are used to compactly represent states obeying the entanglement area law.
key_observables: Nonstabilizerness, quantified by the Stabilizer Entropy ($\alpha$-SE), and the membership of the state in the set of stabilizer states ($	ext{STAB}_N$).
important_parameters: The bond dimension ($D$) of the PEPS, and the Rényi parameter $\alpha \ge 2$.
main_assumptions: The hardness results are established under standard complexity assumptions and apply to the worst-case scenario for the PEPS input model.
figures_summary: The figures illustrate the constructions used in the proofs of computational hardness, specifically showing how to encode zero-testing problems into the PEPS structure.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical relevance of nonstabilizerness, then contrasting the tractability of 1D (MPS) vs. 2D (PEPS) systems, and finally proving the computational hardness results for SE evaluation and stabilizer membership using complexity theory reductions.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous complexity barrier, suggesting that characterizing non-classicality in realistic 2D quantum materials using current tensor network formalisms is computationally intractable for general cases.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. We establish that computing SE of 2D PEPS or just deciding whether a PEPS is a stabilizer state, exactly or approximately, are hard computational tasks for classical and quantum computers. An efficient classical algorithm for either of those tasks would imply the collapse of the polynomial hierarchy, and an efficient quantum algorithm would imply the collapse NP ⊆BQP: both implications are considered highly unlikely.

FIG. 2. Graphical schematizations of the proofs of compu- tational hardness in this work. The main idea is always to encode the number of satisfying assignments of a Boolean cir- cuit in a scalar TN contraction, then embed its result in the 1-qubit amplitude of a specific PEPS.

FIG. 3. Reduction proving C=P-hardness of exact PEPS stabilizer membership. The zero test for a function g ∈GapP is encoded in the amplitude of a single marked qubit of a specifically built PEPS, through the argument of a rational function. The resulting state is a stabilizer state if and only if g(x) = 0.
